outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles or moves the question: the Leinster problem is still open per the current Wikipedia article and the primary sources I could read, no in-window Leinster group was found, and the only in-window Leinster-family paper (Pleşca and Tărnăuceanu, arXiv March 2025, journal November 2025) treats the almost- and quasi-Leinster analogues, not Leinster groups.
problem_asks: (1) Whether there are infinitely many finite groups G, pairwise non-isomorphic, such that |G| equals the sum of the orders of the proper normal subgroups of G (equivalently, the sum over all normal subgroups including G equals 2|G|). That is the whole question: a yes/no on infinitude. It does not ask for a classification, for which orders occur, or for the odd-order or dihedral cases separately.

events.what_happened: Tom Leinster posts 'Perfect numbers and groups' (arXiv math/0104012, sole author, submitted 1 April 2001; Wikipedia's references give it as Eureka 55 (2001), pp. 17-27). He calls a finite group 'perfect' when its order equals the sum of the orders of its proper normal subgroups (the later name is Leinster group). The abstract states that a cyclic group is perfect exactly when its order is perfect, that the only abelian perfect groups are the cyclic ones, and gives some non-abelian perfect groups of even order. No statement on infinitude in the abstract.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only, per the abstract page. Journal version cited by Wikipedia as Eureka 55 (2001).
events.delivers: The definition, the cyclic characterisation (C_n is Leinster iff n is a perfect number), the abelian characterisation (abelian Leinster groups are exactly the cyclic ones of perfect-number order), and a few non-abelian even-order examples. Nothing on whether infinitely many exist.
events.time_since_posted: about 25 years; later papers engage with it (see later_work_cites_it)
events.directly_checkable: The cyclic case is checkable by hand: the proper normal subgroups of C_n have orders the proper divisors of n, so the condition is sigma(n) = 2n, i.e. n perfect.
events.direction: Not a result about the question; it defines the object and sets the question up.

events.what_happened: Tom Leinster asks on MathOverflow (question 54851, posted in 2011 per the bibliography in Baishya 2019 and Wikipedia) whether an odd-order group exists whose order is the sum of the orders of its proper normal subgroups. François Brunault answers with a non-abelian example of order 355433039577. Baishya (arXiv 1911.04829, 2019) says the example was found 'just one day after the question ... was asked', and gives the group as (C127 semidirect C7) x C(3^4 . 11^2 . 19^2 . 113). Wikipedia and Groupprops give the order and call it the smallest known non-abelian Leinster group of odd order. The MathOverflow page itself was not accessible to me (blocked twice), so the posting date, the answer text and the construction are taken from Baishya and secondary pages.
events.delivers: One finite instance: a non-abelian Leinster group of odd order. It adds one instance to the set of known Leinster groups and says nothing about whether there are infinitely many.
events.remains: Infinitude; every other order, including all other odd orders.
events.directly_checkable: The order is checkable by hand: 889 x 399812193 = 355433039577, where 889 = |C127 semidirect C7| and 399812193 = 3^4 . 11^2 . 19^2 . 113 (checked in this record). The Leinster property would be checked by listing normal subgroups in GAP. I did not run that, and no source I read reports such a check.
events.doubts: The construction rests on Baishya (2019) and secondary pages. The MathOverflow answer was not read. The gonitsora.com blog (not opened; search snippet only) describes the same event with a different parametrisation and says it followed the question by a day.
events.direction: An odd-order Leinster group exists: an instance in the 'yes' direction of the infinitude question, but a single finite instance that does not decide it.
events.object: A non-abelian group of odd order 355433039577, given as the semidirect product C127 semidirect C7 times a cyclic group of order 3^4 . 11^2 . 19^2 . 113. Explicit (a construction), not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Tom De Medts and Attila Maróti publish 'Perfect numbers and finite groups' (Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 129 (2013), DOI 10.4171/RSMUP/129-2). They extend the perfect-number notion to finite groups, rename the groups Leinster groups because 'perfect group' already has a standard meaning, and state that they give general theory, examples and related results. Read: the publisher abstract only. Full text not read.
events.delivers: General theory and examples, per the abstract. The abstract states no infinitude result. What the general theory establishes is not known to this record, since the full text was not read.
events.remains: Infinitude, as far as the abstract says.

events.what_happened: Sekhar Jyoti Baishya, 'On Leinster groups of order pqrs', arXiv:1911.04829 (v1, submitted 12 November 2019; only version listed). Proves that no group of order pqrs, for distinct primes p<q<r<s, is Leinster. For order p^2 q r (p<q<r) the Leinster groups are identified as Q20 x C19 or Q28 x C13. Its introduction says: 'It may be mentioned here that, till now it is not known whether there are infinitely many Leinster groups or not', and that 'only one odd order Leinster group is known', found by Brunault shortly after Leinster's MathOverflow question.
events.revisions: arXiv v1 only, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Excludes every order of the form pqrs and classifies Leinster groups of order p^2 q r for all such primes (two groups, of orders 380 and 364). Restricts certain order shapes. Says nothing on infinitude, and states it is open.
events.remains: Infinitude; all orders outside the excluded and classified shapes.
events.directly_checkable: The two order-p^2 q r groups are small and checkable in GAP. I did not check them.
events.doubts: Read through a summarising fetch of ar5iv and the abstract page; the proofs were not read.
events.direction: Restricts which orders can carry Leinster groups; the paper itself reports the infinitude question open.

events.what_happened: OEIS A086792 (orders of Leinster groups; first terms 6, 12, 28, 30, 56, 360, ...) carries a comment that Derek Holt computed the non-abelian orders up to n = 500 and noted that when 2^n - 1 is a Mersenne prime, the group with presentation <x, y | x^(2^n-1) = 1, y^(2^n) = 1, y^-1 x y = x^-1> has order equal to the sum of the orders of its proper normal subgroups. The presentation was taken from a search summary of the OEIS page, not read verbatim. I re-derived it in this record (see directly_checkable). Eric M. Schmidt added terms a(10)-a(17) on 2 May 2014 (per the OEIS page).
events.revisions: The date of Holt's comment is not established. The OEIS revision history was not opened. The only dated edit I found is Schmidt's addition of a(10)-a(17) on 2 May 2014, which does not date the comment.
events.delivers: Conditional on the Mersenne-prime question: for each Mersenne prime p = 2^n - 1 there is a non-abelian Leinster group of order p . 2^n. Different primes give groups of different orders, so infinitely many Mersenne primes would give infinitely many Leinster groups. Unconditionally it gives one Leinster group per known Mersenne prime and says nothing on infinitude.
events.remains: Infinitude, unless and until the infinitude of Mersenne primes is established (an open problem); any other family.
events.directly_checkable: Yes, by hand. Let p = 2^n - 1 be prime, G = <x, y>, |x| = p, |y| = 2^n, y inverts x, so |G| = p . 2^n. A normal subgroup either contains C_p (since C_p has prime order, then it corresponds to a subgroup of G/C_p, which is cyclic of order 2^n), or meets C_p trivially. In the second case it centralises C_p, so lies in C_G(C_p) = <x> x <y^2>, hence in the central cyclic subgroup <y^2> of order 2^(n-1). Proper normal subgroups containing C_p have orders p . 2^k for k = 0..n-1, summing to p . (2^n - 1) = p^2. Those inside <y^2> have orders 2^k for k = 0..n-1, summing to 2^n - 1 = p. Total p^2 + p = p(p+1) = p . 2^n = |G|. For p = 3, 7, 31 this gives the OEIS orders 12, 56, 992. Checked in this record, not in a published source.
events.doubts: Holt's comment is informal and not a published theorem. The OEIS text quotes only the 'if' direction. I did not find a paper discussing this family other than the OEIS comment; the De Medts-Maróti full text was not read, so it may treat the family.
events.direction: Consistent with 'yes', conditionally on an open number-theoretic question. It does not settle the question either way.
events.object: The non-abelian group G = C_p semidirect C_(2^n) with p = 2^n - 1 prime and the generator y of order 2^n inverting the generator x of order p. Order p . 2^n. Explicit (a presentation), not an existence proof.

events.what_happened: Iulia-Cătălina Pleşca and Marius Tărnăuceanu, 'Almost and quasi Leinster groups', arXiv:2503.16884 (v1 21 March 2025; v2 5 April 2025). Define almost Leinster groups (sum of normal-subgroup orders = 2|G| - 1) and quasi-Leinster groups (sum = 2|G| + 1), the analogues of almost-perfect and quasi-perfect numbers. Studies nilpotent cases and non-nilpotent classes (ZM-groups, affine groups, dihedral and dicyclic groups). Journal version: Analele Științifice ale Universității 'Ovidius' Constanța, Seria Matematică 33 (3) 2025, pp. 121-134, DOI 10.2478/auom-2025-0031; submitted 23 Nov 2024, accepted 6 May 2025, online 29 Nov 2025. Its introduction says 'thousands of examples of Leinster groups' were produced by computational programs, citing [13] (Nieuwveld; see that event).
events.revisions: arXiv v1 21 Mar 2025; v2 5 Apr 2025; arXiv comment 'Accepted for publication in An. Științ. Univ. Ovidius Constanța, Ser. Mat.'; journal version online 29 Nov 2025 (DOI 10.2478/auom-2025-0031).
events.delivers: For the analogues only. Per the fetched text: quasi-Leinster ZM-groups exist (Prop. 3.3, Example 3.1, with all r in {2,...,m-1} giving examples in the family treated); the only quasi-Leinster affine group is C2; Aff(F_q) is almost Leinster iff q is prime and q-1 is perfect; dihedral and dicyclic results recover known Leinster results (Remarks 5.1, 6.1-6.2). Per the fetched text it constructs no new Leinster group. Nothing here decides the Leinster question, which is a different condition (sum = 2|G|).
events.remains: The Leinster question entirely; and the almost and quasi classifications in general, which the paper leaves partial (I did not find an explicit list of its open questions).

events.time_since_posted: about 19 months since arXiv v1 (to 11 October 2026); no commentary or citing paper found beyond the journal
events.directly_checkable: The explicit quasi-Leinster ZM-group family can be checked by hand from the normal subgroup lattice of a ZM-group. I did not check it.
events.doubts: (1) Example 1.3 is said to give 44 solutions found with GAP, but the displayed set has four values; this is unreconciled in the fetched text. (2) The paper introduces the variants as having very few known results. (3) The 'thousands' sentence in the introduction cites Nieuwveld's note, whose count is 381 in a search snippet; see the dispute.
events.direction: Cuts toward existence results for the analogues. It does not bear on whether infinitely many Leinster groups exist, since it is a different condition.
events.object: Explicit families of quasi-Leinster ZM-groups (Prop. 3.3, Example 3.1) and almost Leinster affine groups Aff(F_q) for q prime with q-1 perfect. A secondary AI-generated review (not opened) gives the pairs (6,7) and (28,29) as examples; I did not verify them.

events.what_happened: Joris Nieuwveld, 'A note on Leinster groups' (Radboud University student note, hosted on Wieb Bosma's page; per a search snippet written for Bosma's Computer Algebra course in spring 2020). Per the snippet only: reports 381 Leinster groups in total, 'including many new examples', found by a search method that extends candidate parameters; and 293 Leinster groups among the 493 perfect groups of order at most 50 000 in Magma's database, with the note saying these perfect groups are not the Leinster groups as in the literature. The PDF could not be read by the tool, so none of this is verified. Cited by Pleşca and Tărnăuceanu (2025) as the source of 'thousands of examples'.
events.delivers: If the snippet is right, a finite computed set of Leinster groups (381). That adds finitely many instances and says nothing on infinitude.
events.directly_checkable: The computed groups could be re-checked in GAP or Magma. I did not do this.
events.doubts: (1) Count conflict: 381 in the note (per snippet) against 'thousands' in Pleşca and Tărnăuceanu (2025), who cite it. (2) The 293/493 figure concerns a different class (Magma's perfect groups) by its own statement, so the 293 may not count Leinster groups. (3) Student note, not refereed. (4) Not read.
events.direction: Finitely many computed instances. Does not move the infinitude question.

events.what_happened: Marius Tărnăuceanu, 'Finite groups determined by an inequality of the orders of their normal subgroups', arXiv:1805.11691 (submitted 21 May 2018). The visible abstract does not mention Leinster groups, perfect numbers or sums of normal-subgroup orders; it defines a class of finite groups by an inequality on normal subgroup orders. Included because a search snippet describes the inequality as 'sum of normal subgroup orders at most 2|G|' (not verified), which would make the Leinster equality its boundary case.
events.delivers: Not determinable from the abstract. It bears on the question only if the equality case is the Leinster condition, which I did not verify.

events.what_happened: Marco Mantovanelli, 'Certified Minimal-Prime Branch Closures for Odd Perfect Numbers', arXiv:2607.04365 (v1, submitted 5 July 2026; math.GM; independent researcher). Proves branch closures for odd perfect numbers whose smallest prime factor is 5, 7, 11, 13 or 17, by finite checks certified by a released bundle (JSONL, Python verifiers, expected outputs, SHA256). The author states the result 'does not prove nonexistence of odd perfect numbers'; the q = 3 and q >= 19 branches are not covered. Read: the abstract page and the HTML up to Section 11 of about 142 000 characters; the acknowledgements were not reached.
events.revisions: v1 only, per the abstract page.
events.delivers: Nothing about Leinster groups. Odd perfect numbers bear on this problem only through the known equivalence that dihedral Leinster groups correspond one-to-one with odd perfect numbers (per Wikipedia). That concerns the existence of a dihedral Leinster group, not the infinitude question. The paper proves only branch cases of odd-perfect nonexistence.
events.remains: The whole Leinster question; for the odd-perfect neighbour, the q = 3 and q >= 19 branches.

machine_checked.system: Author-released Python verifier scripts and JSONL certificates (not a proof assistant)

events.directly_checkable: The certificate bundle and verifier scripts are said to be released with the paper. I did not run them.
events.doubts: Single author, independent researcher, new preprint. No review found.
events.direction: Neighbouring. Cuts against odd perfect numbers only in its branch cases. Does not bear on the infinitude of Leinster groups.

events.what_happened: Per a search snippet only: a preprint on preprints.ru by Y. Liu, January 2026, claims that odd perfect numbers do not exist. The site itself warns that preprints should not be reported as verified. Not opened.
events.delivers: Unverified claim about odd perfect numbers. If it were correct it would empty the dihedral family, which is a neighbouring question and does not bear on infinitude.
events.doubts: Not opened. Known only from a search summary.

disputes.summary: Pleşca and Tărnăuceanu (2025) say computational programs brought 'thousands of examples of Leinster groups', citing Nieuwveld's 2020 note. A search snippet of that note reports 381 Leinster groups. The note could not be read, so the two figures are unreconciled.

summary: I ran 49 searches (listed below) covering the name and its aliases ('perfect group', 'immaculate group'), arXiv listings, the MathOverflow thread, OEIS, Groupprops, GAP and computation, Lean, lab and AI-result announcements, and expert digests. The current Wikipedia article still reads 'It is unknown whether there are infinitely many Leinster groups', and Baishya's 2019 preprint says the same in its introduction (verbatim in the fetched text, which came through a summarising tool). I found no source, inside or outside the window, that resolves the question or moves any quantity it names. Since 26 January 2024 the only Leinster-family papers are: Pleşca and Tărnăuceanu on almost- and quasi-Leinster groups (arXiv 21 March 2025; journal online 29 November 2025), which address different conditions and construct no new Leinster group per the fetched text; Mantovanelli's July 2026 odd-perfect-number preprint, a neighbouring problem with no Leinster content; and an unopened January 2026 preprints.ru claim about odd perfect numbers. No in-window Leinster group was found. Earlier events: Leinster's definition (arXiv, 1 April 2001); Brunault's odd-order example (MathOverflow question 54851, 2011); De Medts and Maróti (2013); Baishya (Comptes Rendus, online 21 December 2013, results unread; arXiv 2019, restricting orders pqrs and p^2 q r); and a Holt observation recorded in OEIS A086792 whose date I could not establish. The count of computed examples is disputed: Nieuwveld's 2020 student note is the source of the 'thousands' sentence in the 2025 paper, but a search snippet gives 381; I could not read the note. AI: no source I read credits any AI system with Leinster-group mathematics. The one AI lead in the window is a search-summary claim that the acknowledgements of the odd-perfect preprint credit 'ChatGPT 5.5' for LaTeX, literature search and coding. It is unverified, and in any case not load-bearing as described. The OpenAI August 2026 announcement includes a group-theory result on non-sofic groups; that is not about Leinster groups, and the primary OpenAI page refused to load (403), so I relied on secondary coverage for it. My own check, not a source's claim: the Holt family gives a Leinster group for every Mersenne prime 2^n - 1 (order p . 2^n with p = 2^n - 1), and the cyclic Leinster groups are exactly the cyclic groups of perfect order, which by Euclid-Euler correspond to Mersenne primes; the dihedral family corresponds to odd perfect numbers. So both known infinite-looking families are indexed by Mersenne primes (for the even-order cases) or by odd perfect numbers (dihedral), and an unconditional infinitude proof needs either infinitely many Mersenne primes or a new family. No source I read states this dependency explicitly.
competing_reading: (1) The Holt family and cyclic family give an honest conditional route to infinitude, so one could mark the problem as 'reduced to' Mersenne primes rather than open; but the reduction runs only one way (Mersenne infinitude gives Leinster infinitude), so the problem is still open. (2) The computed counts (381, or 'thousands') could be read as evidence that Leinster groups are plentiful and so probably infinite. That is evidence about the expected answer, not a result on infinitude, and finite counts do not move it. (3) The 2025 almost- and quasi-Leinster paper could be counted by a loose reader as progress. Under the scope test it answers a different condition (sums 2|G| - 1 and 2|G| + 1), so it does not count for this question.
what_would_settle_it: (a) The text of Nieuwveld's note (its count, its definition of the 381 and 293 figures, and whether it uses Leinster's condition as stated). (b) MathOverflow question 54851: its posting date, Brunault's answer and the construction. (c) The OEIS A086792 revision history, to date Holt's comment. (d) Full texts of De Medts and Maróti (2013) and Baishya (2014), for any statement on infinitude or on new families. (e) A GAP check that the order-355433039577 group is Leinster (this fixes the odd-order instance; it does not decide infinitude). (f) Any post-2025 paper that either proves a new infinite family or cites the question as still open; I did not find one. (g) The status of the Mersenne-prime and perfect-number questions, which I used as background and did not research.
